ingredients_en: 10 pieces assorted meat (beef, goat, or mix)
1 kg ugu (fluted pumpkin leaves), washed and sliced
instructions_en: Steam stockfish, assorted meat, and dry fish with a little water, sliced onions, one seasoning cube, and salt until tender; reserve the stock.
Boil cocoyam until very soft, peel, and pound to a smooth paste; optionally work in a little palm oil while pounding.
Bring fresh water to a boil, add steamed fish and meat, simmer ~5 minutes, then add palm oil; cook ~2 minutes more.
Stir in pepper, crayfish, and seasoning cubes.
Gradually stir in cocoyam paste and ogiri; simmer ~5 minutes until thickened.
Add ugu and okazi, salt to taste, simmer ~3 minutes until leaves are tender but bright. Serve hot with fufu or garri.
instructions_ig: See okporoko, anụ, na azụ ọkụ na mmiri, alubar, Maggi, nnu ruo mgbe ọ dị mfe; debanye ọsọ.
See ede, kụọ ma ọ bụ mee ka ọ bụrụ paste.
See mmiri, tinye anụ na azụ, see obere; tinye mmanụ aṅụ.
Kwakọta paste ede na ogiri; see ka ọ sie.
Tinye ugu na okazi, nnu, see obere. Nye ya ọkụ.
recipes.cultural_notes_en: From the Owerri people of Imo State: a ceremonial soup thickened with cocoyam and layered with ugu and okazi, often served at special occasions and community gatherings.
recipes.cultural_notes_ig: Ofe ndị Owerri: e ji ede mee ya, na ugu na okazi; a na-esi ya n'emume dị mkpa.

ingredients_en: 2 medium fresh fish (e.g. mackerel or hake)
Generous bunch bitterleaf, washed and squeezed
instructions_en: Grind egusi with part of the crayfish to a fine powder or thick paste.
Steam stockfish and dry fish with water, half the onion, and one cube until tender; reserve broth. Steam fresh fish separately with onion and salt; set aside.
In a large pot, heat palm oil without bleaching; fry ground egusi 3–5 minutes, stirring, until fragrant and clumping.
Add reserved fish broth, remaining crayfish, pepper, stockfish, and dry fish; simmer 10–15 minutes, stirring occasionally.
Stir in washed bitterleaf; cook about 5 minutes. Gently fold in steamed fresh fish; adjust salt. Serve with swallow of choice.
instructions_ig: See okporoko na azụ ọkụ; see azụ ọhụrụ n'ụzọ dị iche.
Kpọọ mmanụ aṅụ, kwade egusi obere.
Tinye ọsọ azụ, eri okporoko, ọse, okporoko, azụ ọkụ; see.
Tinye onugbu; tinye azụ ọhụrụ nwayọọ. Nye ya ọkụ.
recipes.cultural_notes_en: A defining Igbo soup rooted in centuries of melon cultivation. Grinding egusi was traditionally a communal activity among women.
recipes.cultural_notes_ig: Ofe egusi bụ otu n'ime ofe Igbo kachasị amasị ndị mmadụ; ndị inyom ka ha na-ekụ ya ọnụ.
health_tags: Mind sodium in cubes and fish

ingredients_en: 500 g bitter leaf (onugbu), freshly washed and squeezed
8–10 medium cocoyam (soup variety, pinkish or white flesh)
500–700 g beef or goat meat, suitable for slow cooking
1 medium stockfish head (soaked in hot water to soften)
instructions_en: Boil cocoyam until soft; peel while hot and pound to a smooth elastic paste.
Wash and squeeze bitter leaf repeatedly until bitterness is reduced to a pleasant background note.
Steam meat with onion, cube, and salt until tender; add smoked fish and palm oil; boil stock 5–7 minutes.
Drop in cocoyam paste in small scoops; cover and simmer until dissolved; season with crayfish, pepper, and ogiri dissolved in hot broth.
Add bitter leaf; simmer only 3–5 minutes so leaves stay fresh. Serve with fufu, pounded yam, or garri.
instructions_ig: See ede, kụọ ya ka ọ dị sie.
See anụ; tinye azụ na mmanụ aṅụ.
Tinye paste ede; tinye eri okporoko, ọse, ogiri.
Tinye onugbu; see obere. Nye ya ọkụ.
recipes.cultural_notes_en: A ceremonial soup associated with weddings (Igba nkwu), funerals, and the New Yam Festival; the labor of washing bitter leaf and the cost of multiple proteins mark it as a prestige dish.
recipes.cultural_notes_ig: Ọtụtụ mgbe, e nwere ọrụ na onugbu; e ji ya eme emume dị ka igba nkwu na iri ji.

ingredients_en: 250 ml red palm oil (or 2 kitchen spoons)
instructions_en: Wash okra and slice into rounds; set aside.
Season and steam beef and fish separately until partly cooked so fish holds shape.
Boil ~1 L water; add beef 2 minutes, then palm oil.
Add crayfish, pepper, cubes, and salt; cook ~4 minutes.
Gently add fish, then okra; cook ~3 minutes without overcooking to preserve green color.
Stir in chopped ugu; simmer ~3 minutes, adjust salt. Serves ~6 with fufu.
instructions_ig: See anụ na azụ n'ụzọ dị iche.
See mmiri, tinye anụ, tinye mmanụ aṅụ.
recipes.cultural_notes_en: A beloved draw soup whose very name derives from the Igbo word ọkwụrụ; historically cooked in clay pots over open fires. Okra's journey through the trans-Atlantic slave trade influenced dishes such as gumbo.
recipes.cultural_notes_ig: Ofe a na-akpọ draw soup; aha ya sitere n'asụsụ Igbo.

ingredients_en: 3 medium fresh fish, cleaned and cut
400 g dry fish, pre-soaked and deboned
500 g bitter leaf, washed and squeezed
instructions_en: Grind ogbono with crayfish and pepper to a uniform paste.
Steam beef with onion, cube, and salt; add fish and stockfish with water; cook until tender; reserve stock.
Heat palm oil; stir in ogbono paste and fry ~2 minutes; gradually add ~3 L water, stirring constantly to prevent lumps.
Bring to a gentle boil; return proteins; simmer ~15 minutes until the soup thickens and draws.
Add bitter leaf (and optional ugu); adjust salt. Serve hot with fufu, pounded yam, garri, or semovita.
instructions_ig: Tinye mmanụ aṅụ na ogbono; tinye mmiri nwayọọ.
See ruo mgbe ọ dị sara; tinye anụ na azụ.
Tinye onugbu. Nye ya ọkụ na fufu ma ọ bụ garri.
recipes.cultural_notes_en: Made from African bush mango (Irvingia gabonensis) seeds; prized for its mucilaginous draw texture and long communal history. Grinding the seeds was a social gathering.
recipes.cultural_notes_ig: E ji mkpụrụ ogbono mee ya; ọ na-adọrọ mmiri.

ingredients_en: Achara (elephant grass shoots), peeled to creamy core, snapped into ~1-inch pieces
Egusi (melon seeds), ground then pounded into mgbam (small balls/discs)
Osu powder (optional, to bind egusi balls)
Stockfish, smoked fish, beef or shaki
Ground crayfish, yellow/Cameroon pepper, bouillon cubes
instructions_en: Peel achara to the creamy-white core; snap only tender pieces; discard anything woody or bendy.
Pound egusi with optional osu, a pinch of salt, warm water, and pepper until mixture glistens with its own oil; mold into coin-sized discs (mgbam).
Boil meats, stockfish, and dry fish with seasoning cubes and onion until tender; keep plenty of stock.
Add palm oil, crayfish, and pounded pepper; at a rolling boil, drop in mgbam and do not stir for the first 10 minutes.
Once balls are firm, add achara pieces, then okazi; cook ~5–8 minutes. Adjust salt. Serve as a textured Abia-region specialty.
recipes.cultural_notes_en: The 'King of Soups' in the Abia region (Umuahia/Ngwa); the labor of peeling achara and molding mgbam make it a mark of hospitality and prestige.
recipes.cultural_notes_ig: Ofe pụrụ iche n'Abia: achara na mgbam na-egosi ọbịabịa na nzọụkwụ.

ingredients_en: 50 fresh palm fruits, washed and boiled until soft
instructions_en: Pound boiled palm fruits in a large mortar (Ikwe) to separate pulp from kernels; wash pulp with warm water and sieve to extract thick red banger water.
Steam meats, catfish, and stockfish with salt and cubes until tender.
Bring banger water to a vigorous boil; add steamed proteins and simmer ~5 minutes.
Add ground crayfish and pepper; dissolve ogiri in warm water and stir into pot; boil ~10 minutes.
Add sliced okazi first; simmer ~3 minutes, then add ugu; simmer ~3 minutes. Taste and serve with fufu.
instructions_ig: Kụọ mkpụrụ ope, wepụta mmanụ akwu.
See banger water; tinye anụ na azụ.
Tinye okazi na ugu. Nye ya ọkụ.
recipes.cultural_notes_en: Communal extraction of palm-fruit pulp marks celebrations, naming ceremonies, and festivals; pounding in the large wooden mortar (Ikwe) was traditionally women's shared labor.
recipes.cultural_notes_ig: Ofe akwu na-egosi ọbịabịa na emume; ikwe na odo bụ ihe achịkọtara ndị inyom.

ingredients_en: 1 kg okazi leaves, sliced extremely thin
instructions_en: Boil cocoyam, peel while hot, and pound to a lump-free paste.
Shred okazi as finely as possible. Microscopic shreds are the goal.
Boil stockfish and dry fish in 4 L water for at least 30 minutes; add snails and cook ~5 minutes.
Add palm oil, then cocoyam paste in small lumps, stirring to dissolve until soup coats a spoon.
Season with crayfish, pepper, and cubes; dissolve ogiri in a spoonful of hot broth before adding; adjust salt.
Add all okazi; simmer exactly ~5 minutes for tender but vibrant leaves. Serves ~10.
instructions_ig: See okporoko na azụ; tinye ejula.
recipes.cultural_notes_en: Built around Gnetum africanum (Okazi), a wild vine leaf from West African rainforests; associated with Abia and Imo hospitality and special occasions.
recipes.cultural_notes_ig: Aha ahịhịa bụ okazi; a kwesịrị ịkụọ ya nke ọma ka ọ bụrụ dị mma.

ingredients_en: ~10 dried ukpo seeds (Dioclea reflexa), boiled 30 min, shelled, ground to a red paste with a drop of palm oil
instructions_en: Boil ukpo seeds 30 minutes, crack shells, extract inner cream-colored seed; grind with a drop of palm oil to a deep-red paste.
Steam meat, stockfish, and dry fish in a little water ~30 minutes; add ~1.5 L water and boil ~5 minutes.
Add palm oil, crayfish, pepper, and crumbled cube; cook ~3 minutes.
Stir in ukpo paste thoroughly; simmer ~3 minutes until velvety. Thin or thicken with water as needed.
Dissolve ogiri in hot broth and add; adjust salt. On low heat, fold in oha leaves for only 30–60 seconds. Serves ~8.
instructions_ig: See ukpo, kụọ ya na mmanụ.
Tinye mmanụ aṅụ na eri okporoko.
recipes.cultural_notes_en: A celebration and ceremonial soup. Centerpiece at traditional weddings, burial ceremonies, and the New Yam Festival. Skills for preparing ukpo are passed down through families.
recipes.cultural_notes_ig: Ukpo bụ mkpụrụ siri ike; a na-ahụ maka ya n'emume na ọchịchọ n'ofe a.

ingredients_en: 4 wraps ugba (fermented African oil bean seeds)
400 g ahihara (jute mallow/molokhia) leaves, washed and pounded to a pulp
instructions_en: Pound washed ahihara leaves in a mortar until sticky and pulpy (this releases the mucilaginous texture); slice okra and ugu; soak and break fish into pieces.
Optionally steam proteins 10–15 minutes; boil ~1 L water and add them with crayfish, pepper, oil, cubes, and salt.
Simmer ~5 minutes; stir in ugba, sliced okra, and ahihara pulp; simmer ~5 minutes more.
Add ugu; simmer ~5 minutes until bright green. Adjust salt; serve with fufu or swallow of choice.
instructions_ig: Kụọ ahịhịa ahihara; bee ọkwụrụ na ugu.
See anụ na azụ; tinye mmanụ aṅụ na eri okporoko.
recipes.cultural_notes_en: A seasonal jute-mallow soup celebrated for its resilience and adaptability; tied to festivals and family gatherings, and emblematic of the Igbo use of locally available ingredients.
recipes.cultural_notes_ig: Ahihara na-enye ofe ahụ mmiri dị ụtọ; e ji ya eme emume na mkpọkwa.

ingredients_en: Fermented ugba (African oil bean, Pentaclethra macrophylla), properly fermented and sliced
Uziza leaves or scent leaf, sliced
instructions_en: Boil stockfish and any meats with cube, onion, and salt until tender with a flavorful broth.
Add smoked fish and crayfish; stir in palm oil; cook a few minutes until merged.
Stir in ogiri until dissolved.
Optional: stir in smooth cocoyam paste to thicken; add blended peppers and simmer, stirring often.
Fold in ugba and uziza last; do not overcook. Ugba should retain texture. Serve with pounded yam, fufu, or eba.
instructions_ig: Ọ bụrụ na ị chọrọ, tinye ede.
recipes.cultural_notes_en: Fermented oil bean encodes Igbo resourcefulness; historically reserved for title ceremonies and honored guests, and still a symbol of deep cultural hospitality.
recipes.cultural_notes_ig: Ugba bụ nri e ji eme emume na ọbịabịa dị mkpa.

ingredients_en: 1 kg oha leaves (Pterocarpus mildraedii), hand-torn, never cut with a knife
1 kg beef, cut into bite-sized chunks
400 g dry fish, deboned and cleaned
instructions_en: Boil cocoyam until soft; peel while warm and pound to a smooth stretchy paste.
Brown seasoned beef with salt and one cube; add stockfish, dry fish, and 4 cups water; boil until tender.
Add remaining water if needed, palm oil, crayfish, pepper, second cube, and optional ogiri; boil 5–10 minutes until raw oil taste mellows.
Drop cocoyam paste in small lumps; cover to melt, then stir gently until velvety.
Stir in hand-torn oha leaves; simmer only 2–3 minutes to preserve bright color and nutrients. Serve with pounded yam, akpu, or garri.
instructions_ig: Tinye mmanụ aṅụ, eri okporoko, ọse, ogiri.
Tinye ede ka ọ dị sie.
Tinye oha a dọkpụrụ aka; see obere.
recipes.cultural_notes_en: Oha leaves are traditionally torn by hand. Cultural belief holds that metal blades alter the leaf's medicinal potency. Associated with homecoming, new beginnings (Omu), and special occasions.
recipes.cultural_notes_ig: A na-adọkpụ oha site n'aka, ọ bụghị mma ịjị mma bee ya.

ingredients_en: 1 kg catfish, thoroughly cleaned (slime removed with salt, hot water, or lime)
instructions_en: Boil peeled yam until very soft; pound while hot to a smooth elastic paste (or blend with minimal hot water).
Boil 6 cups water with crayfish, pepper, and cubes; drop in small lumps of yam paste and let them melt until broth is velvety.
When ~80% dissolved and thickened, gently add catfish on medium-low heat; avoid vigorous stirring. Shake the pot or nudge with a wooden spatula. Simmer 10–15 minutes.
Hand-tear utazi into the pot; adjust salt; simmer ~3 minutes for herbal aroma. Serve hot with pounded yam, fufu, or eba.
instructions_ig: See ji, kụọ ya ka ọ bụrụ paste.
See mmiri na eri okporoko, ọse; tinye ji ka ọ dị sie.
Tinye utazi a dọkpụrụ aka; dozie nnu.
recipes.cultural_notes_en: Unique for containing no palm oil. Its pale colour earns the name 'White Soup'. Revered as a healing dish for new mothers (Omugwo) and for honoring titled chiefs and special guests.
recipes.cultural_notes_ig: Ofe ọcha a na-eri na Delta Igbo na Anambra; ọ na-enyere omugwo aka.

ingredients_en: Salt and seasoning cubes to taste
instructions_en: Soften stockfish and dry fish with a little water; clean snails thoroughly with lime, salt, or alum.
Grind uziza seeds and uda separately; grind crayfish coarsely; soak ground spices in water, squeeze vigorously, and sieve. Keep the flavored spice water only.
Boil sieved spice water with shokirisho ~15 minutes to allow thickening; remove shokirisho solids.
Add proteins and simmer ~15 minutes; season with crayfish, dry pepper, ogiri, and cubes; cook ~10 minutes.
Add sliced uziza leaves; after only ~5–10 seconds remove pot from heat to preserve volatile oils and colour. Serve with pounded yam or fufu.
instructions_ig: Kụọ uziza na uda; sie mmiri ọsọ ha.
Tinye azụ na ejula; tinye eri okporoko na ogiri.
Tinye ahịhịa uziza; kwụsị ọkụ ngwa ngwa.
recipes.cultural_notes_en: Uziza is celebrated for its peppery warmth and medicinal value; strongly associated with Omugwo postpartum care and believed to stimulate appetite and improve circulation.
recipes.cultural_notes_ig: Ọtụtụ ndị na-ekwu na ofe uziza na-enyere omugwo aka; ọ na-ewu ahụ.

ingredients_en: 1 kg amaranthus (inine), picked and finely sliced
500 g dry fish, deboned and cleaned
instructions_en: Steam beef, stockfish, and dry fish with onion, one cube, and salt until tender.
Add 2 L water; boil ~10 minutes to develop the stock.
Add palm oil, then sprinkle in ground egusi; stir and cook ~5 minutes for a golden base.
Add crayfish, pepper, remaining onion, and second cube; simmer ~6 minutes.
Stir in sliced amaranthus; cook only ~3 minutes. Adjust salt and serve with fufu or eba (~8 people).
recipes.cultural_notes_en: Celebrated for iron-rich greens and lighter body than heavy achi/ofor thickeners; traditionally served to nursing mothers and the elderly for high iron and easy digestibility.
recipes.cultural_notes_ig: Inine na-enye ahụike na ụtọ nri; e ji ya enyere ndị ụmụ nne na ndị okenye.

ingredients_en: 200 g achi (Brachystegia eurycoma seeds), finely ground
1 kg stockfish (head and ear pieces for deeper flavor)
instructions_en: Grind achi seeds to a very fine powder. Smoothness determines soup texture.
Boil stockfish and dry fish in 4 L water ~30 minutes until stockfish softens; add snails, cubes, and salt; continue until snails are tender.
Add palm oil and let incorporate ~2 minutes; stir in pepper, crayfish, and achi vigorously to avoid lumps; cook ~10 minutes until the soup coats the back of a spoon.
Dissolve ogiri in warm broth before adding; boil ~5 minutes to develop the fermented aroma.
Add shredded ugu; simmer ≤3 minutes for vibrant colour. Serve ~10 guests with fufu or eba.
instructions_ig: See okporoko na azụ; tinye ejula.
Tinye mmanụ aṅụ, ọse, eri okporoko, achi.
recipes.cultural_notes_en: Brachystegia eurycoma seeds thicken instantly on contact with hot liquid. Historically prized as a faster alternative to the labor-intensive pounding of cocoyam.
recipes.cultural_notes_ig: Achi na-emezi ofe ngwa ngwa na-abụghị ihe ike dị ka ede.

ingredients_en: Palm fruits (enough to extract ~4 L banga water)
A few drops of red oil (for grinding)
Salt and seasoning cubes to taste
instructions_en: Boil palm fruits until soft; pound in a mortar, wash pulp with 4 L warm water, sieve into a clean pot. This is your banga base.
Thoroughly wash all leaves (scent, utazi, uziza, curry, njanja); grind together with onions, pepper, crayfish, and a drop of red oil until a smooth dark paste forms.
Season beef, stockfish, and dry fish with salt and cubes; steam in their own juices until tender.
Bring banga water to a vigorous boil ~5 minutes; add steamed proteins and cook together ~10 minutes.

Slowly pour in the ground leaf paste; stir thoroughly. As herbs react with the palm oil base the soup will turn its signature dark colour. Stir at intervals ~10 minutes; taste for spice. Serve with pounded yam or fufu.
instructions_ig: Tinye paste ahịhịa; sie ka ọ sie.
recipes.cultural_notes_en: Traditionally served to nursing mothers to aid cleansing and to elders at special celebrations; the dark colour comes from blended aromatic leaves oxidising in the palm oil base.
recipes.cultural_notes_ig: A na-esi ofe ojii maka omugwo na emume ndị okenye.

ingredients_en: 500 g groundnuts (peanuts), roasted or raw, ground to a fine powder (or paste with a little water)
1 kg beef, goat meat, or shaki/tripe
500 g dry fish, deboned and cleaned
instructions_en: Grind groundnuts to fine powder or blend with a little water into a paste; process crayfish and peppers together.
Steam meat, stockfish, and dry fish with some onion, one cube, and salt until tender; reserve the stock.
In a clean pot, warm palm oil; add groundnut powder/paste and fry ~3 minutes, stirring constantly to remove raw taste.
Slowly pour in 2 L water including meat stock; stir well, cover, and boil ~30 minutes until oil rises and soup thickens.
Add steamed proteins; simmer ~5 minutes; add crayfish, pepper, remaining cubes, onion, and salt; boil ~10 minutes.
Add washed bitter leaf; cook ~5 minutes. Adjust seasoning. Serve with fufu, pounded yam, or eba.
instructions_ig: Kụọ ahịhịa igwe; kụọ eri okporoko na ọse.
Kwade mmanụ aṅụ; tinye ahịhịa igwe.
Tinye anụ na azụ; tinye eri okporoko na onugbu.
recipes.cultural_notes_en: Prepared after peanut harvest and often paired with bitter leaf to balance the natural sweetness of the nuts; a cherished alternative to egusi soup in communities where peanuts are a primary crop.
recipes.cultural_notes_ig: E ji ya eme emume mgbe a haa ahịhịa igwe; ọ na-arụ ọrụ dị ka ofe egusi.

ingredients_en: 3 kg goat meat (leg and shoulder), cut into bite-sized chunks
400 g fresh pepper (atarodo), adjust to taste
4 ehuru seeds (calabash nutmeg), toasted and ground
100 g lemon grass, tied in a knot
instructions_en: Wash goat meat thoroughly; place in stockpot with onions, a pinch of salt, and 2 L water; cover and cook on medium-high ~30 minutes to tenderize and build stock.
Toast and peel ehuru; grind with fresh peppers until a paste forms.
Add ground pepper-and-ehuru paste, seasoning cubes, and tied lemon grass; simmer 10–15 minutes until aromas penetrate the meat.
Add sliced scent leaf and utazi; cook only ~2 minutes to wilt and release oils.
Adjust salt; remove lemon grass knot; serve hot in bowls. Pairs traditionally with chilled palm wine. Serves 10.
instructions_ig: See anụ ewu na alubar na mmiri ~30 min.
Tinye nchanwu na utazi; see obere.
recipes.cultural_notes_en: A cultural staple for welcoming honored guests and marking title-taking ceremonies; also a standard restorative meal during Omugwo postpartum care. Ehuru and utazi are believed to aid digestion and provide warmth.
recipes.cultural_notes_ig: E na-esi ya maka ọbịabịa dị mkpa na omugwo.

ingredients_en: 1 kg catfish, cut into steaks, cleaned with salt or lime to remove slime
200 g uda seeds (Negro pepper), ground coarsely
200 g lemon grass (bundle or finely chopped)
instructions_en: Clean catfish steaks thoroughly with salt, hot water, or lime until skin feels squeaky-clean.
Grind uda seeds (remove inner bitter seeds if preferred) and uziza seeds to a coarse powder; blend or pound fresh peppers.
Place cleaned fish in pot; add water to just submerge; bring to a boil ~10 minutes without stirring vigorously (shake the pot instead).
Add ground uda, uziza, and pepper; simmer ~5 minutes to infuse the fish.
Add salt, scent leaves, and lemon grass; simmer a final ~5 minutes. Serve hot in bowls with palm wine or as a standalone appetizer.
instructions_ig: Kụọ uda na uziza; bee ọse.
Tinye nnu, nchanwu, ọchịọchị. Nye ya ọkụ.
recipes.cultural_notes_en: The primary dish served to women after childbirth (Omugwo) in riverine Igbo communities (Onitsha, Oguta, Asaba); the potent spices are believed to aid recovery and stimulate appetite.
recipes.cultural_notes_ig: E na-enye omugwo ofe a; ọ na-ewu ahụ.

ingredients_en: 2 kg puna yam, peeled and cubed
Fresh pepper to taste (atarodo or Cameroon pepper)
Utazi or scent leaves, finely shredded
ingredients_ig: Anụ ewu ma ọ bụ azụ 1 kg
instructions_en: If using goat meat: steam with salt, one cube, and a little onion until ~70% tender. (If using catfish: wash thoroughly; add later at step 3.)
Add peeled yam chunks to the pot; pour in enough water to submerge (~1.5–2 L); cover and boil on medium-high heat.
When water boils and yams begin softening, add crayfish, remaining cube, and crushed pepper. (Add catfish now if using.)
Allow yam edges to slough off naturally. The released starch thickens the broth. Mash one or two chunks against the side if needed.
Stir in shredded utazi or scent leaves; simmer just ~60 seconds to wilt. Serve hot in deep bowls; broth is meant to be drunk after the solids.
instructions_ig: Mee ka ji sie ruo mgbe ọ dị sie na ọsọ aṅụrọ.
Tinye utazi; see obere. Nye ya ọkụ.
recipes.cultural_notes_en: The gold standard of Omugwo postpartum care: believed to stimulate milk production and restore energy; also a warming comfort meal for cold rainy seasons and honored guests.
recipes.cultural_notes_ig: Ji mmiri ọkụ bụ nri omugwo kachasị; ọ na-enyere ndị ụmụ nne aka.

ingredients_en: Small piece of ntu-ncha (potash) for emulsifying oil
instructions_en: Clean corn; soak overnight in plenty of water. In the morning, drain, add fresh water, and boil ~10 minutes until kernels are tender but firm.
Cook beans in a separate pot until completely soft.
Dissolve potash in a little water; in a separate bowl add palm oil then slowly stir in the potash solution until the oil turns thick and bright orange-yellow (ncha emulsion).
Stir ground red pepper, sliced utazi, and a pinch of salt into the emulsion.
Combine cooked corn and beans with the oil-spice mixture; stir well over low heat. Adjust salt and serve hot. Serves ~8.
instructions_ig: Tinye ọse na utazi na ncha.
Jikọta oka na agwa na ncha.
recipes.cultural_notes_en: A communal harvest-season meal traditionally cooked in large clay pots for farmers returning from the fields; corn and beans together provide a complete protein source.
recipes.cultural_notes_ig: E ji ya enye ndị ọrụ ugbo nri n'oge ịhachaa oka.

ingredients_en: ~4 kg puna yam (2 tubers), peeled and cubed
Fresh or dry pepper to taste (habanero preferred)
2–3 cups chopped vegetables (ugu, utazi, or scent leaf)
instructions_en: Peel and cube yam; rinse in cold water to remove excess starch.
Place yam in pot; add water to barely cover. Bring to a boil on medium-high heat.
After ~10 minutes (when yam starts to soften), add onion, pepper, crayfish, and salt; cover and cook ~3–5 minutes.
Add palm oil; use wooden spoon to mash a few pieces of yam against the pot side to thicken the sauce.
Add chopped vegetables; simmer ≤5 minutes so they stay vibrant. Taste and adjust. Serve hot with fried fish or palm wine.
instructions_ig: Tinye mmanụ aṅụ; see ka ọ dị sara.
recipes.cultural_notes_en: The soulful everyday comfort food of the Igbo; the one-pot harvest meal representing hospitality and the richness of the land, with the New Yam Festival's grand pounded yam as its ceremonial counterpart.
recipes.cultural_notes_ig: Ji awai bụ nri ụlọ na-amasị ndị Igbo.

ingredients_en: 2 kg unripe plantains, peeled and cubed
1 medium dry/smoked fish, cleaned and deboned
instructions_en: Peel and cube plantains uniformly; soak dry fish in hot salt water, clean, debone, and break into chunks.
Place plantains in pot; add water to barely cover; bring to a rolling boil 2–5 minutes until starch starts to cloud the water.
Add dry fish chunks, palm oil, crayfish, onions, and cubes. Do not stir immediately. Let oil emulsify into the water.
Cover and simmer ~5–10 minutes until plantains soften and sauce thickens.
Add scent leaves and a pinch of salt; simmer a final ~3 minutes. Serve warm. Porridge thickens further on standing. Serves ~3.
instructions_ig: Tinye azụ, mmanụ aṅụ, eri okporoko.
recipes.cultural_notes_en: A farmer's one-pot meal; unripe plantain is specifically chosen over ripe for its complex carbohydrates and lower sugar. Traditionally recommended for those managing blood sugar.
recipes.cultural_notes_ig: E na-ahọrọ unere akịdị maka ọ dị mma maka ọbara sukari.

instructions_en: Wash akidi; boil until tender; leave in cooking water overnight to mellow the skins.
The next morning, discard brownish water; refresh with clean water; boil ~10 minutes. Drain completely.
Dissolve potash in a little warm water and strain. Pour palm oil into a clean pot; slowly add potash solution, stirring vigorously until oil turns creamy yellow-orange (ncha emulsion).
Stir in pepper, crayfish, ugba, cooked egusi, and a pinch of salt until evenly combined.
Gradually add drained akidi; mix until every bean is coated. Adjust salt and serve with palm wine.
instructions_ig: See akidi; lee ya n'mmiri oché.
recipes.cultural_notes_en: A symbol of resilience and agricultural prowess; cultivated alongside yam and cassava as a vital protein source during the 'hungry season' before the main yam harvest.
recipes.cultural_notes_ig: Akidi na-enyere ndị Igbo aka n'oge ọụrụ mgbe agwa si ite.

instructions_en: Peel cocoyam, wash thoroughly in cold water; cut into medium chunks, not too small or they dissolve completely.
Place in pot; add water to almost cover; boil on medium-high ~8–10 minutes until firm-tender.
Add palm oil, crayfish, dry pepper, and salt; boil together ~3–5 minutes to cook out raw oil taste.
Add scent leaf and utazi; stir with wooden spatula. Stirring releases starch and thickens the liquid into porridge.
Simmer a final ~3 minutes. Adjust salt; serve hot in a wide bowl. Serves ~5.
instructions_ig: Tinye mmanụ aṅụ na eri okporoko.
recipes.cultural_notes_en: Considered a 'female crop' in contrast to the 'king' yam; slow simmering transforms cocoyam's thick starch into a creamy, soul-warming meal. Aromatic herbs like scent leaf and utazi add both flavour and medicinal value.
recipes.cultural_notes_ig: Ede bụ ihe ndị inyom na-asị ka ọ dị; ọ na-enye nri ụlọ.

ingredients_en: 1 kg (4 cups) brown or honey beans
instructions_en: Pick through beans; rinse 2–3 times; soak ≥30 minutes to reduce cooking time and bloating.
Grind pepper, crayfish, garlic, ginger, and turmeric to a textured paste; slice onions and scent leaves separately.
Boil beans in water 45–60 minutes until soft enough to mash between two fingers.
Once thick and porridge-like, add palm oil, sliced onions, the ground paste, scent leaves, and salt; stir well.
Simmer ~10 minutes so oil and spices distribute evenly; mash a few spoons of beans to adjust consistency. Serves ~5 with plantains, garri, or steamed yams.
instructions_ig: Kụọ ọse, eri okporoko, garliki na jinja.
See agwa ruo mgbe ọ dị nro.
Tinye mmanụ aṅụ, ọse, nchanwu, nnu.
recipes.cultural_notes_en: A cornerstone of Igbo home cooking; the use of scent leaf (nchanwu) is distinctive and believed to aid digestion. Beans were prized protein especially when meat was reserved for ceremonies.
recipes.cultural_notes_ig: Agwa bụ nri e ji nọọ n'ụlọ; nchanwu na-enyere mmiri ya aka.

recipes.name_en: Beans and Unripe Plantain (Agwa na Ogede)
ingredients_en: 1 kg unripe plantain, peeled and cubed
instructions_en: Pick through beans; wash well. Optional: parboil ~10 minutes, drain, and start with fresh water.
Boil beans in fresh water 60–90 minutes until easily mashed between fingers; keep enough liquid in the pot.
Add cubed unripe plantains; cook ~10 minutes. The starch from the plantain thickens the bean broth.
Add ground crayfish, pepper/ginger/garlic paste, sliced onions, and palm oil; stir gently; simmer ~5–7 minutes.
Add shredded scent leaves and salt; stir vigorously to create a creamy texture; simmer ~5 minutes on low heat. Serve warm.
instructions_ig: Tinye mmanụ aṅụ na eri okporoko.
recipes.cultural_notes_en: Represents the agricultural synergy of Igboland; beans supply protein and unripe plantain supplies iron and complex carbohydrates. A deliberately heavy, sustaining meal for farmers and laborers.
recipes.cultural_notes_ig: Agwa na unere akịdị bụ nri dị arọ maka ndị ọrụ.

instructions_en: Clean fio-fio; boil water ~20 minutes; add fio-fio and soak ~20 minutes; drain. This reduces gas. Boil again in fresh salted water ~3 hours, topping up as needed, until soft.
Add cubed yam; cook ~20 minutes until tender; drain any excess water.
In a frying pan, heat palm oil; add onions, pepper, crayfish, ugba, utazi, and cubes; sauté ~5 minutes.
Pour hot sauce over cooked fio-fio and yam; mix thoroughly until every pea and yam chunk is coated.
Taste; adjust salt; serve warm. Traditionally in a wooden bowl.
instructions_ig: Sacha fio-fio; see ya iri iri.
recipes.cultural_notes_en: A legendary legume of Enugu, Anambra, and Ebonyi regions; a 'resilience crop' that sustained farmers during droughts and became a cultural marker of the Igbo harvest season.
recipes.cultural_notes_ig: Fio-fio bụ mkpụrụ ndụ dị ike; ọ na-enyere ndị Igbo aka n'oge ihe ọjọọ.

ingredients_en: 400 g dry fish, deboned and flaked
Plantain leaves or food-grade nylon for wrapping
instructions_en: Grind and sieve bambara nuts to a smooth flour.
Grind pepper and crayfish; slice onions and scent leaves; soak dry fish in warm salted water, debone.
Combine flour with palm oil and salt; rub oil into flour until uniform with no white streaks.
Slowly add warm water, stirring to prevent lumps. Batter should be fluid enough to pour but thick enough to hold 'surprises' in suspension.
Fold in pepper, crayfish, onions, ugba, scent leaves, and fish; stir thoroughly.
Wrap in wilted plantain leaves or nylon; secure with string. Steam over boiling water ~1 hour 30 minutes, refilling water as needed. Check firmness. Serve hot. Serves ~15.
instructions_ig: Chịkọta ya; see na akwụkwọ ogede ~1hr 30min.
recipes.cultural_notes_en: A cultural icon of Enugu State; made from Bambara nut (Vigna subterranea), it was the ultimate traveler's and farmer's food. Dense, portable, and true to its ancient roots.
recipes.cultural_notes_ig: Okpa bụ nri ama ama nke Enugu; e ji ya eme njem.

ingredients_en: 2 kg ukwa (Treculia africana) seeds, fresh or dried
500 g dry fish (mangala or smoked catfish)
Tiny pinch of potash/ngu (optional, as tenderizer)
instructions_en: Wash ukwa thoroughly in a sieve-bowl. Removing all sand is critical. Cover with water (2–3 inches above seeds); add optional potash; boil 45–60 minutes until soft but not mushy.
Add dry fish and crayfish; simmer ~10 minutes to release oils into the broth.
Add onion, pounded pepper, and ugba; crumble in cubes; stir gently.
Add salt; simmer ~5–10 minutes until liquid thickens into a rich sauce.
Rest 5 minutes before serving (thickens further). Serves ~10.
instructions_ig: Sacha ukwa nke ọma; see ya ~45–60 min.
Tinye nnu; see ka ọ dị sara.
recipes.cultural_notes_en: Considered a prestige delicacy historically reserved for titled men, elders, and significant ceremonies. The labor of extracting seeds from the large fruit head makes serving ukwa a mark of deep respect for a guest.
recipes.cultural_notes_ig: Ukwa bụ nri ọgọ; e ji ya asọpụrụ ndị okenye na ọbịabịa dị mkpa.

ingredients_en: 1 tsp potash (akanwu), dissolved in warm water and strained
1 cup each soaked shredded stockfish and dry fish
Pepper and 2 seasoning cubes to taste
½ cup utazi leaves for garnish
instructions_en: Soak abacha in cold or lukewarm water 2–3 minutes only; drain immediately so it does not go mushy.
Whisk strained potash water into palm oil in one direction until the oil turns thick and yellow (ncha sauce).
Mix in crayfish, pepper, crushed cubes, salt, and shredded fish so they absorb the sauce.
Add ugba, then drained abacha; toss until every strand is coated (add only a little extra oil if dry, not water).
Fold in some sliced onions; plate and garnish with utazi leaves and garden egg slices.
instructions_ig: Jiri akanwu mee sauce na mmanụ aṅụ.
Tinye eri okporoko, ọse, Maggi, azụ.
Tinye ugba na abacha; kwakọta ha.
recipes.cultural_notes_en: Originally a snack served at village gatherings, it has evolved into a sophisticated meal. The preserved cassava technique enabled long-term food storage across seasons.
recipes.cultural_notes_ig: Abacha bụ nri e ji akpọ African salad; e ji ya mee emume.

ingredients_en: 1 kg cow foot/leg, cut into bite-sized chunks
1 tsp edible potash (akanwu), dissolved in ½ cup warm water and strained
1 medium onion (half for boiling, half for garnish)
Seasoning cubes and salt to taste
Handful utazi leaves, finely shredded for garnish
instructions_en: Wash cow foot; pressure-cook (or boil) with sliced onion, cubes, and salt until tender but still chewy with skin. Leave very little stock.
Dissolve potash in ½ cup warm water; strain through a fine sieve.
Pour palm oil into a clean pot or bowl; slowly add potash water, stirring consistently in one direction until oil thickens and turns opaque creamy yellow (ngwo-ngwo sauce).
Stir in crayfish, pepper, cubes, and ugba until well incorporated.
Add warm cooked cow foot; toss vigorously so every piece is coated; place on low heat ~2–3 minutes to warm through.
Heap into a small wooden mortar (serving bowl); garnish with raw onion rings and shredded utazi.
instructions_ig: Mee ngwo-ngwo sauce na mmanụ aṅụ.
Nye na nkwobi bowl; tinye utazi.
recipes.cultural_notes_en: A social dish originating in local bars and joints, shared among elders during evening gatherings with palm wine. It has since become a centerpiece at Igbo weddings and high-end restaurants globally.
recipes.cultural_notes_ig: Nkwobi bụ nri a na-eri na ọchịchọ na emume.

ingredients_en: 2 medium onions (one for boiling, one for garnish)
Seasoning cubes and salt to taste
instructions_en: Wash goat head pieces; place in pot with sliced onion, cubes, and salt; add water to cover and cook until very tender but not falling off the bone. Separate meat from stock; reserve some concentrated stock.
Dissolve potash in a little water; strain. Pour palm oil into a clean pot or large bowl; slowly add potash water, stirring in one direction until oil turns to a thick creamy yellow paste (ncha).
Add crayfish, pounded pepper, and a little concentrated stock; stir well. If brain is included, mash into the sauce for extra richness.
Add cooked goat head pieces; place on very low heat ~2–3 minutes to warm through and absorb flavours. Do not over-cook.
Dish into wooden mortars (Ikwa bowls); garnish with utazi shreds and raw onion rings. Best with palm wine or chilled malt.
instructions_ig: Nye na Ikwa bowl; tinye utazi.
recipes.cultural_notes_en: A celebratory dish served to honored guests, titled men, and at traditional weddings and naming ceremonies. The velvety potash-and-palm-oil sauce is a hallmark of Igbo culinary craft.
recipes.cultural_notes_ig: Isi ewu bụ nri ọgọ na emume Igbo.

ingredients_en: 5 cups long-grain rice, parboiled and washed
ingredients_ig: Mmiri ma ọ bụ ọsọ 5 cups
instructions_en: Blend tomatoes, bell peppers, and scotch bonnet until smooth.
Heat oil in a heavy-bottomed pot; sauté onions until translucent; fry tomato paste ~3–5 minutes.
Pour in blended mixture; cook ~10–15 minutes, stirring occasionally, until water evaporates and oil separates from the sauce.
Add cubes, salt, and optional spices; pour in stock; bring to a rolling boil.

Add washed rice; stir gently; cover pot with aluminium foil then the lid to trap steam. Cook on low heat ~20–30 minutes. For the 'Igbo smoky' finish, raise heat the last 2 minutes until a slight char aroma rises. Serve with fried plantain and meat.
instructions_ig: See na ụdị mmiri na ọkụ ọ dị.
recipes.cultural_notes_en: Though originating from the Jolof Empire, Igbo Jollof became the quintessential party rice. A symbol of celebration at weddings (Igba Nkwu) and naming ceremonies. The iconic smoky bottom (achieved over firewood) is a point of pride.
recipes.cultural_notes_ig: Osikapa jollof bụ nri emume Igbo kachasị ama ama.

ingredients_en: 400 g bonga fish (smoked), deboned and shredded
instructions_en: Grind pepper and crayfish; slice onions and pumpkin leaves; soak and shred bonga fish.
Boil yam in salted water ~20 minutes until firm-tender; 5 minutes before done, place sliced leaves on top to steam.
Drain; separate yam and leaves.
Heat palm oil without bleaching; sauté onion, then pepper, crayfish, salt, and bonga fish ~2 minutes.
Toss yam in the sauce, add steamed leaves, mix gently and finish quickly so greens stay bright. Serves ~5.
instructions_ig: Kụọ ọse na eri okporoko; bee ugboguru.
See ji; see ugboguru n'elu ya obere.
Chụọ mmiri; kewaa ji na ahịhịa.
recipes.cultural_notes_en: A 'tossed' harvest dish. The yam pieces remain distinct, unlike mashed pottage. Traditionally prepared during harvest when pumpkin leaves were abundant, representing the intersection of the king crop and the backyard garden.
recipes.cultural_notes_ig: Ọ bụghị ji ọwụwa dị ka porridge; ji a na-aga n'ụzọ ya.

ingredients_en: 4 cups honey or brown beans, soaked and peeled
Salt and 2 seasoning cubes to taste
Uma (Thaumatococcus) leaves, foil pouches, or ramekins for wrapping
instructions_en: Soak beans ~10 minutes; rub to loosen skins; rinse repeatedly until beans are white and clean.
Blend peeled beans with tatashe and onions using minimal water until completely smooth.
Pour batter into a large bowl; incorporate vegetable oil, crayfish, salt, and crumbled cubes; stir slowly in one direction to aerate. This makes the pudding fluffy.
Slowly add warm water until consistency resembles thick pancake batter.
Fill leaf cones or greased containers; add an egg slice to each; seal tightly.
Steam over boiling water on a rack ~45–60 minutes. Test with a toothpick. Serves ~8.
recipes.cultural_notes_en: A staple of Igbo hospitality, central to traditional weddings (Igba Nkwu) and naming ceremonies. Steaming in Uma leaves imparts an irreplaceable earthy aroma that modern containers cannot replicate.
recipes.cultural_notes_ig: Moi-moi bụ nri emume Igbo; akwụkwọ Uma na-enye ya ọdọdọ pụrụ iche.

ingredients_en: 4 cups black-eyed beans, soaked and peeled until white
instructions_en: Soak beans ~10–20 minutes; rub between palms to descale skins; rinse until beans are clean and white.
Blend beans with onions and peppers using minimum water. The paste must be very thick.
Pour into a large bowl; whisk or stir vigorously in circular motion ~5–10 minutes to incorporate air bubbles for fluffiness.
Add salt just before frying (not earlier. Salt deflates the bubbles).
Heat oil on medium-high. Test: a drop of paste should sizzle and float immediately. Scoop paste and drop gently into oil; fry in batches. Do not crowd the pan.
Fry until golden brown on both sides; drain on paper towels. Serve hot with ogi (pap) or agidi.
instructions_ig: Tụgharịa batter ka o dị ọhụụ.
recipes.cultural_notes_en: A mainstay of communal breakfast culture across Igbo market days (Afor, Eke, Orie, Nkwo); the rhythmic pounding to aerate the batter was a morning ritual before blenders became widespread.
recipes.cultural_notes_ig: Akara bụ nri ọ́ụ́tụ́tụ́ e ji eje ahịa Igbo.

ingredients_en: 10 cups dry white or yellow maize
Plantain or Uma leaves for wrapping
ingredients_ig: Akwụkwọ ogede ma ọ bụ Uma
instructions_en: Sort maize; parboil 15 minutes; sieve hot water. Soak in fresh water overnight (or up to 2 days), changing water every 24 hours for fermentation.
Rinse fermented corn; grind to a very fine slurry; sieve through muslin cloth into a large bowl, removing all chaff.
Let starch settle at the bottom; decant clear water on top; squeeze remaining moisture out through muslin. You now have raw akamu/agidi paste.
Mix paste with a little clean water until milk-like. Cook on medium heat, stirring continuously for ~10 minutes as it thickens from opaque white to glossy off-white.
Wilt plantain leaves over a flame; pour hot paste into leaves or greased tins; fold and seal; cool at room temperature until firm. Serve with tomato stew, beans, or akara.
instructions_ig: Sacha oka; see obere; tụọ ya n'mmiri ọchęchọ.
Kụọ ya; sieve na chiffon cloth.
See na ite, na-akwakọta mgbe niile.
Chịkọta na akwụkwọ; chere ka ọ sie.
recipes.cultural_notes_en: A versatile staple bridging snack and main course; fermentation enhances nutritional absorption by breaking down phytic acid. Serves as the first solid food for Igbo infants.
recipes.cultural_notes_ig: Agidi bụ nri ndị Igbo ji amalite ịṅụ nri.

ingredients_en: 8 cups dry yellow maize, 'half-ground' to a coarse gritty texture
Plantain or Etere leaves for wrapping
ingredients_ig: Oka ọcha 8 cups (a kụọ ọkara ya)
Akwụkwọ ogede ma ọ bụ etere
instructions_en: Clean maize; wash thoroughly. Half-grind with mortar/pestle or instruct a mill to 'break' not fully grind. Coarse gritty pieces are the goal.
Wilt leaves over a low flame to make them flexible.
Mix half-ground maize with palm oil, dry pepper, and salt; add warm water gradually until a thick scoopable paste forms. It should be slightly over-seasoned as steaming reduces intensity.
Wrap portions in wilted leaves; fold and secure.
Line pot with spare leaf stalks; add ~2 inches of water; arrange wraps; steam ~60 minutes. Check firmness; rest 10 minutes before serving. Serves ~10.
recipes.cultural_notes_en: A hearty field-lunch wrap for farmers; the deliberate coarse grind gives a distinct gritty-sweet-savoury texture unlike fine-flour Moi-Moi, showcasing Igbo ingenuity with simple maize.
recipes.cultural_notes_ig: Mkporoshi oka bụ nri ọrụ ugbo; a na-ede ya n'akwụkwọ.

ingredients_en: 10 cups dried corn (yellow for tart ogi, or white for standard)
Water (for soaking, grinding, sifting, and cooking)
Sugar, milk, and optional ginger or cloves to serve
instructions_en: Sort corn; wash; soak 3 days, changing water every 24 hours to ferment.
Wash fermented corn; grind to an extremely fine slurry; sieve through muslin cloth to extract smooth starch.
Let starch settle; decant top water; squeeze out moisture through muslin. This is raw Akamu.
To serve: thin desired amount with a little room-temperature water until smooth; slowly pour boiling water in a circular motion until it thickens and changes colour.
Add sugar and milk to taste. Serve hot with akara, fried plantain, or Moi-Moi.
instructions_ig: Hichaa na mmiri ọkụ ka ọ sie.
recipes.cultural_notes_en: The first solid food for Igbo infants and a soothing meal for the elderly or ill. Fermentation enhances mineral absorption. Sharing the grinding process was a communal morning ritual for women.
recipes.cultural_notes_ig: Akamu bụ nri ndị ụmụaka na ndị ọria; ọ na-enye ahụike.

instructions_en: Whisk flour, sugar, salt, and yeast together in a large bowl.
Gradually pour in warm water; mix by hand to a stretchy batter. Thicker than pancake batter, thinner than bread dough.
Cover tightly; leave in a warm draft-free place ~1 hour until batter doubles and shows air bubbles.
Heat oil on medium. Test: a drop of batter should sizzle and rise immediately.
Squeeze batter between thumb and index finger to form spheres; drop into hot oil. Fry in batches, turning until rich golden brown. Drain on paper towels. Serve warm.
recipes.cultural_notes_en: Once a quick roadside breakfast for laborers, puff-puff is now an essential 'guest-welcoming' snack at Igbo traditional weddings, funerals, and naming ceremonies.
recipes.cultural_notes_ig: Puff-puff bụ nri ụzọ e ji anọdụ ọchịchọ na emume.

ingredients_en: ½ cup whole milk (optional, for richer dough)
1 L vegetable oil for deep frying
instructions_en: Sift flour; add sugar and nutmeg. Rub butter into flour until it resembles coarse breadcrumbs.
Make a well; add whisked eggs and milk; incorporate until a firm non-sticky dough forms; knead ~2–3 minutes.
Roll dough to ~¼ inch thickness in portions; cut into small ~½ inch squares; dust lightly with flour.
Heat oil on medium. Test: a piece of dough should sizzle and rise immediately.
Fry in batches, stirring for even browning, until deep golden. Drain on paper towels; cool completely before storing in an airtight container.
instructions_ig: Tinye akwa na mmiri ọ̀lụ̀; knead.
Tọpụ dough; bee ya; bee ya ka ọ bụrụ ntakiri.
recipes.cultural_notes_en: Adapted from colonial-era shortbread, chin-chin became a symbol of communal sharing at agricultural milestones and family reunions. Its long shelf life made it ideal for festive gatherings.
recipes.cultural_notes_ig: Chin-chin bụ nri e ji emume na nchekwaa oge ọchịchọ.

ingredients_en: Optional: pinch of nutmeg or splash of vanilla extract
instructions_en: Sift flour; add sugar, salt, and yeast; whisk until evenly distributed.
Make a well; add lukewarm water (not boiling. It kills the yeast); mix until a thick slightly-sticky dough forms.
Cover; proof in a warm place ~1 hour until doubled.
Heat oil on medium. Test: a small piece of dough should sizzle and rise to the top slowly.
Grease palms; scoop dough and roll into golf-ball-sized spheres; drop gently into oil; fry ~5–7 minutes, turning occasionally, until deep golden. Drain on paper towels.
instructions_ig: Mee bọl; sie na mmanụ ọkụ.
recipes.cultural_notes_en: The denser, crustier cousin of puff-puff; a 'Mama Put' and market staple popular with students and traders as a filling on-the-go meal across Southeastern Nigeria.
recipes.cultural_notes_ig: Buns bụ nri ụzọ dị arọ n'ahịa; ọ na-aṅụ ahụ.

instructions_en: Sift flour; add sugar, salt, baking powder, and optional nutmeg; whisk together.
Create a well; add whisked eggs and warm milk; mix until a tacky dough forms. Knead ~5–8 minutes on a floured surface until smooth and elastic.
Roll dough to ~1.5 cm thickness; stamp out circles with a glass rim and a bottle cap for the hole.
Heat oil on medium. Test: a piece of dough should sizzle and rise immediately.
Fry rings ~2–3 minutes per side until deep golden. Drain; toss in granulated sugar while warm.
instructions_ig: Tinye akwa na mmiri ọ̀lụ̀; knead.
recipes.cultural_notes_en: Arrived through colonial contact; became a bakery staple in Igbo cities (Enugu, Onitsha, Aba) from the 1970s–80s, and is now a standard item on the 'Item 7' refreshment menu at Igbo weddings and naming ceremonies.
recipes.cultural_notes_ig: Dọnọt bụ nri ọchịchọ na 'item 7' n'emume Igbo.

ingredients_en: 2 eggs, beaten (one for dough binding, one for egg wash)
¼ cup cold milk or water
Seasoning cube and salt to taste
instructions_en: Filling: sauté onions until translucent; add flaked fish, pepper, salt, and crumbled cube; stir-fry ~3–5 minutes. Set aside to cool completely.
Pastry: sift flour; rub in cold margarine until mixture resembles breadcrumbs; add cold milk/water gradually until a stiff dough forms. Do not over-knead.
Roll dough to ~5 mm on a floured surface; cut circles with a cutter or small pot lid.
Place a spoonful of cooled filling in the centre; fold into a semi-circle; crimp edges firmly with a fork.
Bake at 180 °C, brushed with egg wash, ~25–30 minutes until golden. Or deep-fry for 'market square' street style. Serve warm.
instructions_ig: Mee filling: sie alubar, tinye azụ na ọse.
Mee dough: rubụ bọta na flour.
recipes.cultural_notes_en: An Igbo adaptation of colonial British pastry; spiced mackerel filling replaced British creamy casserole style. Refined by market vendors in Onitsha and Aba; now a wedding and New Yam Festival after-party staple.
recipes.cultural_notes_ig: E mepụtara pai azụ na ahịa Onitsha na Aba.

ingredients_en: 1 tbsp flour mixed with water (slurry, to bind filling)
2 eggs, beaten (one for sealing, one for egg wash)
instructions_en: Filling: heat oil; sauté onions; brown minced meat; add carrots, potato, thyme, cube, salt, and a splash of water; cook until vegetables are tender; stir in flour slurry to make a moist gravy. Cool completely.
Crust: sift flour and baking powder; rub in cold margarine to breadcrumb texture; add chilled water and knead gently to a stiff dough; refrigerate 20 minutes to relax gluten.
Preheat oven to 180 °C. Roll dough to ~5 mm; cut circles with a bowl lid.
Place filling in centre; brush edges with beaten egg; fold to a half-moon; crimp with a fork; poke top once for steam.
Brush tops with egg wash; bake ~25–30 minutes until golden. Serve with malt drink or fruit juice.
instructions_ig: Mee filling; chere ka ọ jịo.
recipes.cultural_notes_en: Introduced during the colonial era and now an iconic 'small chops' item at every Igbo celebration in Enugu and Onitsha bakeries. A perfectly crumbly crust that yields slightly on the bite is the mark of a skilled baker.
recipes.cultural_notes_ig: Pai anụ bụ nri ọchịchọ na becker n'obodo Igbo.

ingredients_en: 5 large hard-boiled eggs, peeled and cooled
½ cup whole milk (adjust for dough consistency)
ingredients_ig: Akwa 5 (a sie ruo mgbe ọ siri ike)
instructions_en: Boil eggs ~10 minutes; peel and set aside to cool completely and dry.
Whisk together flour, sugar, salt, and baking powder; rub in margarine to breadcrumb texture.
Add milk gradually; knead gently until a smooth non-sticky dough forms.
Divide into 5 balls; roll each flat; place a boiled egg in the centre; wrap dough around it and pinch to seal; roll between palms to a sphere.
Heat oil on medium. Test: a small piece should sizzle and rise slowly. Fry rolls ~5–7 minutes, turning, until rich golden brown. Drain on paper towels. Serve warm.
instructions_ig: See akwa; chere ka ha jịo.
Sie na mmanụ ọkụ; chụọ mmanụ.
recipes.cultural_notes_en: An Igbo street-food classic: the doughnut shell must be a stiff dough (not batter) to properly encase the egg. Evolved from colonial pastry influence into a ceremonial 'small chop' at traditional weddings and community gatherings.
recipes.cultural_notes_ig: Egg roll bụ nri ụzọ e ji eme emume Igbo.

recipes.name_en: Ikpo Oka / Epiti (Corn and Plantain Pudding)
ingredients_en: 1.5 kg dry corn, half-ground to a smooth paste
Seasoning cubes and salt to taste
Etere (Thaumatococcus) leaves or plantain leaves for wrapping
ingredients_ig: Akwụkwọ etere ma ọ bụ ogede
instructions_en: Parboil corn ~20 minutes (not fully cooked); sieve and cool.
Blend drained corn with peeled ripe plantains, peppers, crayfish, and onions to a smooth thick paste (do not add excess water. Plantain moisture helps).
Transfer to a bowl; stir in palm oil until colour is uniform.
Debone bonga fish; break into small chunks; fold into batter.
Add cubes and salt; taste. Should be slightly over-seasoned as steaming reduces intensity.
Wrap in wilted Etere or plantain leaves; steam ~1 hour. Check firmness. Serve warm as a heavy breakfast or hearty lunch.
recipes.cultural_notes_en: A seasonal harvest-time staple that uses the natural sweetness of ripe plantains alongside earthy corn; the sweet-and-savory profile is unique among Igbo wrapped foods.
recipes.cultural_notes_ig: Epiti bụ nri e ji eme mgbe a haa oka na ogede.
